source.title: Open-sci-ref-0.02: open reference baselines for reproducible language model and dataset comparison
source.authors: Marianna Nezhurina; Harsh Raj; Victor May; J. Franke; Taishi Nakamura; Timur Carstensen; Niccolò Ajroldi; Ville Komulainen; David Salinas; J. Jitsev

record.tranche_reason: The study reports downstream benchmark trajectories across model scales and training tokens, a different measure from the held-out cross-entropy loss in the original scaling-law work.
record.gate_note: The study says its trajectories are reference comparisons, not a full scaling-law study. It reports downstream results across scales, including a dataset whose relative performance changes substantially with scale. It does not report held-out pretraining-loss scaling fits or compute-optimal allocations. Cited scaling-law results are not the study's own results.
record.test_reason: The controlled suite reports its own downstream 11-task averages across four model scales (0.13B–1.7B) and token budgets (50B, 300B, 1T) under a fixed recipe. These results bear on V6 qualitatively, though no prediction rule is fitted. There are no held-out loss scaling fits, compute-optimal estimates, architecture-shape sweeps at fixed size, or other modalities.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors present reference trajectories, not full scaling laws, and say the measurements are too sparse for compute-optimal frontiers or precise extrapolation. Dataset rankings are broadly stable across scale, except MixtureVitae, which rises substantially. Their recipe on 1T Nemotron-CC-HQ tokens matches SmolLM2-1.7B with about 11× less compute. Steep trends across external models can be artifacts of weak small-scale points (EuroLLM-1.7B).
record.recipe_differences: This is a controlled dataset-comparison suite with downstream evaluations, not a reproduction of the original held-out-loss fitting and extrapolation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Relative dataset ranking changes with model scale; MixtureVitae is the stated exception to broadly stable rankings among conventional web-oriented references.

fits_no_version.finding: Dataset rankings are broadly stable across scales for conventional web datasets. MixtureVitae, however, moves from near the bottom at 0.13B to the HPLT/FineWeb-Edu range at 1.7B, so a single small-scale proxy run would misrank it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small-scale proxy runs reliably predict the relative ranking of pretraining datasets at larger scale.

record.problems: The study itself notes that it covers only four model scales up to 1.7B parameters and selected token budgets, and is insufficient for full scaling-law estimation or precise extrapolation. The relevant trajectory is described qualitatively in the text without exact values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Endpoint benchmark tables compare datasets or external models but do not test downstream predictability across scale; context-length and dropout results likewise do not test the versions' stated loss relationships. No held-out-loss scaling results are reported.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss reported against parameters, tokens or compute.
No loss fits on small runs extrapolated to larger runs; authors say the data are too sparse for this.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count. Context length and dropout were compared only on downstream averages, not loss.
No quantitative prediction of downstream scores from scale or from pretraining loss; no fitted trend or held-out prediction test.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents. The warning that a weak small-scale point can steepen a trend is illustrated only with external, uncontrolled models (EuroLLM).

missing.what: Absolute 11-task average downstream performance as a function of model scale (0.13B–1.7B at 300B tokens) and tokens (300B vs 1T at 1.7B), per dataset
Per-task signal at 1.7B: MMLU and some other tasks near chance or uninformative, while ARC, HellaSwag and LAMBADA give clear gains

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 limits_scope verdict rested on dataset rank change. That is not V6's claim, which concerns models improving predictably with scale. The verdicts given here are text-based and qualitative, because the study fits no trend. The EuroLLM comparison uses external uncontrolled models and is not the study's own scaling result.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is reported as a function of parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
The study does not fit loss curves on smaller runs and test predictions on larger runs.
The study does not identify or measure compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.

It does not compare depth, width, or other architectures at a fixed parameter count using loss. Context-length and dropout comparisons use downstream evaluations, not the loss measure named in this version.
The experiments concern text pretraining; they do not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
The study reports downstream benchmark trajectories but does not test a quantitative prediction rule relating downstream performance to held-out pretraining loss.

The study cautions that weak small-scale points can make trends look steep, but does not test how fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with fitting choices, nor whether held-out-loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: open-sci-ref-0.02 reference runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream 11-task-average trajectories across model scales.
rows.measure: Relative rank on the 11-task downstream average across model scales
rows.baseline: Other reference datasets; exact comparison values not stated
rows.value: MixtureVitae moves from near the bottom at 0.13B to the HPLT/FineWeb-Edu range at 1.7B.
rows.note: Aggregate trajectory finding across the four stated model scales; the text describes the rank shift but gives no exact values for this trajectory.
rows.check: The row measures relative dataset rank across scales, not whether a model's downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss. Whether small proxy runs predict dataset rankings is a different question (data-choice proxy reliability). MixtureVitae's own score still rises with scale. Moved to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: 11-task average, controlled open-sci-ref runs, 0.13B–1.7B and 50B–1T tokens
relationships.reason: Text-based, since no row records it. Average downstream performance rises steadily with model scale and tokens, e.g. FineWeb-Edu 1.7B goes from .57 at 300B to .60 at 1T (Fig 2, Fig 5, Table 3). No predictive fit is tested.
relationships.display_finding: Average performance increased with size and tokens, with FineWeb-Edu 1.7B improving from 0.57 at 300B tokens to 0.60 at 1T, without testing predictive fits.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: 11-task average, controlled open-sci-ref runs, 0.13B–1.7B and 50B–1T tokens
source_check.reason: Figures 2 and 5 show qualitative downstream scaling trends. Table 3 gives FineWeb-Edu-1.7B averages of .57 at 300B tokens and .60 at 1T. Support is limited to observed trends; predictive extrapolation is untested. These results need dedicated rows.

relationships.condition: Individual tasks such as MMLU at ≤1.7B scale
relationships.reason: Text-based, since no row records it. Authors say MMLU and some other tasks give limited or insufficient signal at this scale: FineWeb-Edu MMLU is .26 at 300B, near chance (Fig 3, Table 3).
relationships.display_finding: FineWeb-Edu achieved 0.26 MMLU accuracy at 300B tokens, near chance, providing limited signal for distinguishing datasets at 1.7B parameters.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Individual tasks such as MMLU at ≤1.7B scale
source_check.reason: Section 4.1 and Figure 3 describe limited signal for distinguishing datasets at 1.7B, not a demonstrated failure of downstream scaling predictability. FineWeb-Edu's .26 MMLU endpoint alone does not establish a scaling limitation; Table 3 reports .32 at 1T tokens.
